# 旅行·地点·建筑 {.unnumbered}



> 本主题共 10 篇语境短文。每篇把一批旧词织进一个场景：**左栏**读短文（目标词加粗），**右栏**常驻该篇生词释义，可先猜后对照。



### A Traveler's Notebook: From Shoreline to City Core

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="57%"}
Arriving by ferry, I watched the **gulf** narrow as we docked near the harbor mouth. The old **isle** sat just offshore — a rocky silhouette against the pale morning sky — while ahead, the city's **CBD** rose in glass and steel, the kind of skyline that makes a traveler feel small in the best possible way. A concrete **ramp** led from the pier up to the promenade, where a row of **pole**s flew the national colors.

I had booked a room in what the listing called a "character flat," though *character* turned out to mean a single **pane** of warped glass in the window and a **crum** barely wide enough for one. The place sat off a **byway** two blocks from the main **blvd.**, wedged between a laundromat and a shop selling souvenir **atlas** collections. Not exactly a grand **abode**, but cheap. Down the hall was a shared lounge — really just a **nook** carved out under the staircase — and beyond that a dim **den** that the owner used for storage. I had slept in worse: a canvas **hut** on the coastal trail in **Peru**, a converted grain **crib** near **Burma**'s border, a windowless room above a **pit** mine in the highlands. Compared with those, this was luxury.

By afternoon I was out. The conference I had come for was held in an **arena**-style hall with a tiered **dais** at the front; a wide **aisle** ran down the center, dividing the audience in two. The speaker climbed **aloft** onto the platform and spread her annotated maps — **loci** of ancient settlement patterns — across the table. She traced the **Troy** campaign, paused on the archaeology of **Kyiv**, touched briefly on **Gaza**, and ended with **Orem** in Utah as an unlikely parallel case. Afterward, a reception moved outside to a rooftop **deck** overlooking the river. Someone had flooded the lower courtyard to make a temporary **rink**, and children were already lacing skates. I found a corner, balanced my drink on the rail, and watched the city settle into evening — every **acre** of it lit, restless, alive.
:::

### A Slow Journey Through Old Stones and New Shores

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="57%"}
Leaving the **exurb** behind, we boarded a **liner** at dawn. The ship's lower **cabin** smelled of salt and timber, and somewhere below the waterline lay a **crypt**-like cargo hold no passenger dared explore. By afternoon we had traced the **Indus** valley on a map pinned above the bunk, tracing the ancient **locus** of civilization with a fingertip.

We docked at a port edged by a **fjord**, its dark cliffs split by a narrow **chasm** that plunged out of sight. A **cleft** in the rock above the **entry** to the old town had been carved into a **porch**, where **Irish** monks once read and **Czech** merchants once bartered. We hired a **moped** and rode past a crumbling **manor**, through a **metro** underpass lit by bare bulbs, and out into a broad **patio** behind a hillside **lodge**. A **cubby** off the kitchen held walking maps; a **depot** on the edge of town stocked fuel and dried food.

Further south — deep into country that felt like **Dixie** by heat alone — we reached **Luxor** at dusk. The city's **Greek**-columned museum overlooked a courtyard where families still **dwell** in converted **condo** blocks whose **metro**-facing facades bore faded murals of **Libya** and **Qatar**. A lone caretaker sat in a **igloo**-shaped guard post outside an old **crypt**. Back at the guesthouse, a small **cubby** in the wall served as a mailbox, its single **entry** slot labeled in both Arabic and the local **hsien** script. We fell asleep to the sound of buses reversing into the **depot** below, dreaming of **Fargo** winters and ice-road **cabin** life — a world away from this warm stone **porch** and its ancient, **cleft** sky.

### From the Aegean to the Atrium: Notes of a Wandering Eye

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="57%"}
Standing on a cliff above the **Aegean**, where the water shimmered in every shade of blue the eye could name, it was easy to forget that the morning had begun in a cramped **sedan** on a pot-holed road cutting through **rural** scrubland. The driver, a cheerful man who moonlighted as a **trike** repairman, pointed **afield** toward a ridge and said simply, "**Delphi**."

We arrived to find the sanctuary wrapped in mist. The **aerial** view from the upper terrace — if you can call two hours of switchback climbing an ascent — opened a **vista** of olive groves falling away toward the gulf below. Back in town I checked into a modest **suite** at a guesthouse whose owner kept a **cellar** stocked with retsina and a small **alcove** off the lobby lined with antique maps. One showed the full **realm** of the old Ottoman provinces: **Syria**, **Tibet**, **Dakota** (someone had clearly improvised), and a coastline labeled **Baltic** where the **Aegean** should have been. Cartography, apparently, was not his strong **Swiss** suit.

The next morning took us to the shell of a Roman **villa** on the edge of a **campus** that a German university had been excavating for a decade. The central **atrium** still had its mosaic floor, cracked by a long-ago **crater** — whether volcanic or from a wartime shell nobody could agree. Beyond it ran a covered **arcade** of columns, and tucked into one end was a **duplex** structure: a lower storage hall that once functioned as a grain cellar, and an upper sleeping room reached by a narrow stair. The **closet**-sized **sewer** outlet at the base of the wall reminded you that even grand architecture has its unglamorous infrastructure.

We ended the circuit in **Athens**, then flew north — briefly over **Beirut**, cloud-covered, then onward. The **faroff** lights of a coastal city, seen through the plane window, looked like a slow-burning **Baltic** constellation. I thought of **Selma** and her offhand remark at the airport: "Every place is someone else's **castle**." The **trike** driver would have agreed.

### Wandering Far and Near

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="57%"}
The itinerary began modestly enough: a few nights at a **hostel** outside **Madrid**, then a slow train east toward the **Venice** of the north. Our group had flown in through **France**, rented a car from a roadside **garage**, and spent the first afternoon hunting for a decent **locale** to drop our bags. We found one at last — a cluster of **lodges** set above a shallow **valley**, their stone walls still warm from the afternoon sun.

From there we followed the **resort** towns southward, through the kind of **remote** hill country where the only sign of life is a shepherd's silhouette on a ridge. The road dipped into a long **tunnel**, emerged beside a sluggish canal, and delivered us to a medieval **hamlet** of perhaps forty houses. A stone **mantel** inside the inn bore the names of travelers who had rested there for centuries.

The second leg took us farther: a **safari** camp in the **tropic**s, where the **gutter** of a night rainstorm ran in silver threads off the reed roof; a **ghetto** neighborhood in a port city that had quietly become its most painterly **venue** for street art; a river settlement beside the **Tigris** that reminded us, impossibly, of illustrations from a book on ancient **Persia**. We crossed into **Quebec** one grey Tuesday, then looped down through **Nevada** and the adobe **Pueblo** villages baking in the desert light. The contrast with **Sweden**'s long summer evenings — where we had been only weeks before — was almost comic.

Somewhere between **Guyana**'s jungle lodges and a layover in **Kuwait** on the way to **Israel**, the trip stopped feeling like a checklist and became something else: a slow accumulation of **venues**, **locales**, and accidental discoveries that no itinerary had planned. Even the **Serbia** detour, added on a whim, gave us a hilltop fortress with a view down into a silver **valley** we had not expected to love. The **Mexico** leg came last — a colonial city, a **galley** kitchen in a rented apartment, coffee on the roof at six in the morning.

### Wanderers, Walls, and Windows

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="57%"}
The **voyage** began at dawn, when the last stars were still fading above the **hilltop** monastery. We had studied maps of **Eurasia** for months — from the ancient streets of **Ephesus** to the river bends of **Babylon** — yet nothing prepares you for the moment a **far-off** skyline finally resolves into stone and smoke.

Our first stop was a **cottage** tucked inside a walled **enclave** at the edge of the old city. A narrow **archway** led us in, its keystone worn smooth by centuries of passing hands. Above the **doorway**, someone had painted a small sun. Inside, the **ceiling** was low and vaulted, and a crooked **chimney** rose from the kitchen hearth like a punctuation mark against the morning sky. We shared a **cubicle**-sized room on the upper floor, where a **balcony** jutted out over a lane of herb sellers and pigeon coops.

By afternoon we had crossed into a rougher district — former **barrack** buildings repurposed into studios, each one occupying a modest **acreage** of courtyard — and stood before the grandest **edifice** on the square: a civic hall whose **African** granite columns had been shipped, so the plaque read, from a quarry near **Baghdad**. The architect had been born in **Cologne**, trained in **Belgium**, and had spent a restless decade moving between **Georgia**, **Bolivia**, **Ecuador**, **Jamaica**, **Croatia**, and **Belarus** before settling here. On the steps, a guide gestured toward **yonder** ridge where **Lebanon** cedars lined the old Crusader wall, and pointed out that the street below had once been the main road into the district of **Bethany**.

### Traces of Civilization, Echoes of Place

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="57%"}
Long before continents drifted apart from the primordial **pangaea**, human beings were already drawn to water. The ancient **Athenian** philosopher from **Miletus** understood this: settle near a shore, and trade will follow. That instinct has never faded. Travelers today still trace those old routes — crossing the **Adriatic**, skimming the **Atlantic**, gliding down the **Yangtze**, threading through the locks of **Ontario** — as if re-stitching the seams of the world.

On land, the architecture tells the same story of arrival and shelter. In a cobbled quarter of **Tribeca**, a converted **mansion** rises behind a wrought-iron gate, its upper **terrace** overlooking a **corridor** of narrow streets below. A **passage** cuts through the building's base, dark and cool, leading to a courtyard where the old **taverns** once filled with sailors off the docks. Deeper beneath the city, **tunnels** carry thousands of commuters past foundations that predate the **suburbs** by centuries. Step into an **elevator**, rise twelve floors, and the **pathway** from street to sky takes less than a minute — yet every surface you touch was once raw earth.

The same layering appears wherever you travel. In **Calcutta**, in **Myanmar**, on the **Yucatan** coast, along the shores of **Tunisia** and **Liberia**, across the plains of **Uruguay** and the forested hills of **Vermont** and **Arkansas**, in the university towns of **Berkeley** and the corporate towers of the **Emirates** — buildings absorb the climate and the culture that raised them. A simple **shelter** in **Oceania** and a glass tower in **Delaware** are, at root, the same impulse: stake a place, keep the elements out, make room for living.

### Wandering from the Baltic to the Tropics

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="57%"}
The journey began in **Tallinn**, where everything felt unmistakably **Estonian** — amber-lit cobblestones, medieval spires, and a courtyard **pavilion** that had somehow survived every **Prussian** incursion and **Flanders**-style trade war the centuries could throw at it. Standing at the **junction** of the old town and the harbour, I traced the city's **interior** lanes by the glow of each **lamppost**, their halos dissolving into the fog rolling off the **maritime** Baltic. A sleek **monorail** ran silently overhead, threading between copper rooftops — an incongruous modernism in a city that felt frozen in amber.

From there the itinerary leapt across **landmass**es with the logic only long-haul flights possess. **Montreal** in autumn, where the **Northern** light turns every stone building sepia by four o'clock. A detour through **Portland** and on to **Oklahoma** and **Nebraska**, state signs blurring across flat **plateaus** that seemed to go on longer than Paraguay itself — though **Paraguay**, too, appeared later on the map, wedged between rivers I had to look up. Somewhere in a **Pasadena** side street I found a small **monument** to the city's citrus-boom past, the kind of **premises** that doubles as a heritage site and a gift shop. In **Portugal** the same impulse manifests as **obelisks** placed at the centre of every provincial square, pointing at a sky equally indifferent to glory and to rain.

The second half of the trip belonged to heat. In **Lebanon** — or rather in the **Lebanese** hill towns above Beirut — the roads narrowed to threads along the ridgeline, and the **panorama** at dusk stretched all the way to Cyprus. Flying south over the horn of Africa, we passed above **Ethiopia** and banked toward **Ndjamena**, **Chad**'s capital, before continuing to the coast. The **Maldives** leg was pure contrast: every structure raised on sand and coral, no **lavatory** more than a few metres from the sea, the entire **maritime** logic of the islands expressed in the way buildings turned their backs to the noon sun and opened toward the lagoon. I thought of the **Manitoba** lakes I'd seen months before — cold, grey, enormous — and of **Pakistan**'s mountain roads, where hairpin bends unfolded into fresh **panorama**s every hundred metres. Geography, I decided, is just the slow **interior** monologue of the planet, and travel is the only way to listen.

### A Long Day on the Road

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="57%"}
The **itinerary** had looked manageable on paper: a morning **excursion** to the hilltop ruins, an afternoon drift along the broad **boulevard** that ribboned through the old quarter, and a quick stop at the **gymnasium** converted into a youth hostel near the **dormitory** district. But travel, as always, rewrote the plan.

We reached the site at midday. The ruins sat at a commanding **elevation**, their broken **colonnade** casting sharp shadows across a sun-bleached **courtyard**. In the **vicinity**, a row of **terraced** houses clung to the slope like a sentence written sideways. A rusted **downspout** rattled against one wall. Further down the path lay a small **graveyard**, its stones worn smooth, and below that, half-hidden by overgrowth, the entrance to the **catacombs** — narrow, cool, and oddly peaceful. Before we descended, someone found the **restroom** tucked behind the ticket booth, a mercy after four hours in the sun.

By evening we were far from plan. A mechanical delay had left the group **stranded** at a provincial junction, one bag short and one **stowaway** cat richer — the animal had slipped aboard the van outside a market in the lowlands. We scrolled through photos: the **bleachers** of an abandoned stadium in **Guatemala**, a **mausoleum** modeled on the one the word itself came from, a **houseboat** moored on a canal whose surface caught the last light perfectly. Tomorrow the **escalator** in the city-center station would carry us back up to the main concourse; tonight we spread maps on the floor of a café near the **Euphrates** bend and traced a slower route — through **Slovenia**, past the chalk cliffs of **Hampshire**, maybe even as far as **Milwaukee** or the granite face of **Rushmore**. Somewhere outside **Bethlehem** or **Suriname**, perhaps, we would find the **secluded** courtyard that every traveler is quietly looking for, the one that does not appear in any **Lexington** guidebook but reveals itself only to the **stranded** and the unhurried.

### A Journey Without a Fixed Map

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="57%"}
The old harbor town had long **territory** no official chart had ever captured — its alleys were frankly **uncharted**, and the **stairwell** of the fifteenth-century watchtower still bore the faint geometric reliefs that any **Babylonian** mason would have recognized as kin to the ziggurats of the Euphrates plain. A rusted **turnstile** at the tower's base was the only concession to modernity, clicking reluctantly each time a visitor passed.

Further east, the **expedition** pushed into **subarctic** highlands where the air tasted of iron and snow. The research team — a **Lithuanian** geologist, two **Portuguese** cartographers, and a guide born to the **indigenous** community of the plateau — had spent weeks tracking the **whereabout** of a lost monastic complex. The **castellated** walls they finally found stood at a remarkable **elevation**, commanding a view of the entire **archipelago** that spread below like shards of green glass in grey water. A **provincial** museum back in the capital had once catalogued the site, but the records were lost during a period of mass **emigration**: whole families forced to **repatriate** to coastal cities, leaving the highlands emptied.

In the lowlands, the contrasts grew sharper. **Mogadishu**'s rebuilt seafront, **Singapore**'s layered transit halls, the worn boulevard of **Louisville** beside the Ohio, the campus sprawl of **Chapel Hill**, a cattle **squattage** outside a **Tennessee** valley town, the oil-stained suburbs of **Venezuela** — each place carried its own logic of **occupancy**, its own answer to the question of who belonged and who was merely passing through. In a sleek **Bangladesh** guesthouse, the kitchen's **backsplash** was tiled with a mosaic of the **Tyrrhenian** coastline — someone's homesick tribute to a sea they would never reach again. On the top floor a faded poster advertised charter flights to **Kyrgyzstan**, destination of the latest wave of **venezuelan** expats chasing work across a world whose borders the old maps of **Singapore**'s colonial era had never imagined.

### Layovers, Lobbies, and Lost Luggage

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="57%"}
The old train car had been divided into a single **compartment** for families, its **window-pane** fogged with the breath of restless children. A printed map on the wall traced the route **in all directions** — east toward the coast, west into the plains — with **demarcation** lines showing which regions fell under separate rail authorities. It felt, somehow, like standing at the edge of **Mesopotamia**: ancient, unhurried, and very far from home.

After a connecting flight via the **Philippines**, the terminal at **Tallahassee** looked almost sleepy by comparison. The **baggage claim** carousel turned in slow circles, depositing suitcases onto the belt with a mechanical patience that matched the afternoon heat outside. A fellow traveler, returning to a **condominium** near the water, said she had done this same loop — **Massachusetts** to Florida and back — every winter for a decade. She had also lived briefly in **Connecticut** and, before that, a rental in **Pennsylvania** that she remembered mainly for its drafty halls and a beautiful **mantelpiece** above a fireplace nobody ever lit.

The lobby of the heritage hotel carried traces of older architectures: the clay plaster typical of **Mesoamerica**, the carved wooden headers you find across **Saskatchewan**, even a small brass plaque noting that the original owners had held diplomatic ties with **Saudi Arabia**. In one corner, a framed print showed **Montgomeryshire** in autumn, its hills impossibly green. Nobody seemed to know why it was there. Nobody asked. Travelers rarely do — they arrive, they look, they leave, scattering **in all directions** again before the place has a chance to explain itself.
